extraction.name: FLORES-101
extraction.description: A high-quality evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences sourced from English Wikimedia content and professionally translated into 101 languages. Translations are multilingually aligned, supporting evaluation of 10,100 translation directions. Metadata includes source URLs, topics, sub-topics, and flags for hyperlinked entities and images.
extraction.creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan
extraction.inLanguage: English source sentences and translations into 101 languages, listed with ISO 639-3 codes, language families, and scripts in Table 4.
extraction.citeAs: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, and Angela Fan. 2021. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1, 6 June 2021.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Construction had three phases: sourcing English sentences, running pilot experiments to select translation providers and establish translation and evaluation workflows, and translating across all target languages. Articles were selected at random from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage. Ten laboratory annotators manually selected typically 3–5 contiguous sentences from one paragraph per article, avoiding very short or malformed sentences. Paragraph locations were balanced approximately equally between article beginnings, middles, and ends. Source URLs, topics, and flags for hyperlinked entities and images were also extracted. Professional language service providers translated the sentences, with editing, automated checks, independent human evaluation, and iterative re-translation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Publicly and freely available English Wikimedia text from Wikinews, an international news collection; Wikijunior, age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12; and WikiVoyage, a travel guide covering travel tips, food, and destinations. Approximately one third of the sentences came from each source.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The same English sentences were professionally translated across target languages to produce multilingually aligned data. Documents were divided into dev, devtest, and test splits. Table 1 reports 997 dev sentences, 1012 devtest sentences, and 992 test sentences.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Selection excluded segments with very short or malformed sentences. Translations underwent automated language identification, source-copy detection, length-difference checks, language-model fluency checks, and similarity checks against commercial translation-engine outputs. Sets with more than 10% of sentences violating the engine-copy criteria required re-translation before human evaluation. Failed checks triggered re-translation until verification passed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Professional translators at an initial language service provider translated each language, and different translators within that provider edited the translations. An independent provider assessed quality and supplied sentence-level and language-level linguistic feedback. Evaluators identified grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register errors, assigning minor, major, or critical severity. Evaluators were encouraged to pay particular attention to unnatural translations. Insufficient-quality translations were returned to the original provider for re-translation and, when required, further human evaluation. Sentences were also manually assigned one of ten sub-topics: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, or travel.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Identified error types and severities were tallied into a per-language Translation Quality Score on a 0–100 scale. Pilot experiments established an acceptable score of 90%. All included languages met this threshold; several additional languages were excluded after failing to meet it following re-translation. Approximately half of the included languages scored above 95%. Mistranslation was the largest error category. Two translation and re-translation workflows showed negligible quality differences, so the operationally simpler workflow using the original translation provider for re-translation was selected.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Sentence selection involved ten laboratory annotators: six male and four female. They were researchers, including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers, originally from East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America. Translations were produced by professional translators working through language service providers; separate providers performed human quality evaluation.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SentencePiece BLEU (spBLEU) was used for automated similarity checks to detect translations potentially copied from public translation engines. Language identification and language-model fluency checks were also implemented, but their software names are not specified. Final translations were human-produced, and guidelines prohibited using translation engines.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors hope to expand language coverage and make the test set available to community evaluation efforts and shared tasks. Dev and devtest are publicly downloadable; the test set is planned to remain accessible only through a public evaluation server. No update schedule, deprecation policy, or explicit maintenance assignment is specified.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to foster progress in low-resource machine translation, benefiting speakers whose native languages are poorly supported or unsupported by popular translation engines. It enables evaluation of traditionally neglected, regionally relevant non-English language pairs and is intended to support development of direct translation between African languages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: All original sentences were sourced in English, so non-English source sentences used for evaluation are human translations and may exhibit translationese, including overly literal or awkward phrasing. Paragraph positions were balanced to avoid document-structure bias. Automated checks were introduced to reduce copying from commercial translation engines, which could otherwise unfairly advantage those engines under reference-based evaluation. Most sentences concern world travel, with substantial coverage of science, politics, and crime.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Non-English evaluation sources are translated rather than originally authored in those languages, creating a translationese caveat. Coverage is limited to the selected Wikimedia sources and included languages; several additional languages could not meet the quality threshold after re-translation. Translation quality varies across languages despite all included languages meeting the 90% threshold. Qualified translators are scarce for low-resource languages, and differences in proficiency or local conventions can affect quality and consistency.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of low-resource and many-to-many multilingual machine translation, including direct translation versus English-centric pivoting; document-level and multimodal translation; sentence and document classification; language identification; and multilingual domain adaptation. Dev is intended for hyper-parameter tuning, devtest for testing during development, and the unreleased test split for evaluation through a public server and shared tasks. Restricting test access is intended to ensure equivalent model assessment and reduce test-set overfitting.
